title: HashMap null key — one null key, multiple null values
shortTitle: HashMap null key — one null key, multiple null values

s1_definition.profdef: `HashMap` permits exactly ONE `null` key and any number of `null` values. The null key is stored in bucket 0 because `HashMap` special-cases it: instead of calling `key.hashCode()` (which would throw `NullPointerException`), it assigns hash 0. Because a `Map` cannot hold duplicate keys, putting a second entry under the null key simply overwrites the first.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the bank's filing cabinet where each drawer is labelled by account number. One special drawer has NO label at all (the null key) — the bank allows exactly one such unlabelled drawer. You can store anything inside it, and you can even store "nothing" (a null value) in many labelled drawers, but there is only ever one unlabelled drawer.
s1_definition.oneliner: HashMap allows one null key (stored in bucket 0) and many null values; a second null-key put overwrites the first.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `HashMap` permits exactly ONE `null` key and any number of `null` values. The null key is stored in bucket 0 because `HashMap` special-cases it: instead of calling `key.hashCode()` (which would throw `NullPointerException`), it assigns hash 0. Because a `Map` cannot hold duplicate keys, putting a second entry under the null key simply overwrites the first.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of the bank's filing cabinet where each drawer is labelled by account number. One special drawer has NO label at all (the null key) — the bank allows exactly one such unlabelled drawer. You can store anything inside it, and you can even store "nothing" (a null value) in many labelled drawers, but there is only ever one unlabelled drawer.

**One line to remember:** HashMap allows one null key (stored in bucket 0) and many null values; a second null-key put overwrites the first.

sections.s3_banking: At the National Bank of India this came up directly when handling the single null key in HashMap. Rajesh holds savings account SAV2001 with a balance of 1,000,000 rupees and Priya holds current account CUR3001 with 250,000 rupees, and the team needed the collection behaviour to be exactly correct so balances and account lists were never wrong. The runnable demo below reproduces the situation and proves the behaviour with a small test.
sections.s5_journey:
The input is a HashMap that receives a null key and several null values.

Step 1: `put(null, 1000000)` computes a hash of 0 and stores the value in bucket 0 as the null-key entry.

Step 2: `put("SAV2001", null)` stores Rajesh's account with a null value, which is allowed.

Step 3: `put(null, 250000)` finds the existing null-key entry in bucket 0 and overwrites its value.

Step 4: `get(null)` returns the latest value, 250000, confirming only one null key exists.

```text
INFO: null key stored in bucket 0
INFO: get(null) returned 250000 (overwritten)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
HashMap allows exactly one null key and any number of null values. The null key is special-cased with a hash of zero and stored in bucket zero, so it never triggers a NullPointerException on put or get.

In our National Bank system I used this when modelling a default fallback balance under a null key while individual accounts such as Rajesh's SAV2001 could legitimately hold a null value meaning 'not yet computed'. I was always careful to remember that Hashtable and ConcurrentHashMap reject nulls, so any code that might migrate to a concurrent map used an explicit sentinel key instead of null.

In an interview I would stress that I always use BigDecimal for money, keep map keys immutable, and pick the collection whose ordering and complexity match the banking access pattern, because in a system that moves real money, choosing the wrong data structure is not a style issue, it is a correctness and reliability issue.
